battle.title: Lock Picking: Mutex vs Semaphore
battle.description: Mutual exclusion, permits and the race conditions they prevent.

questions.text: What is the key conceptual difference between a mutex and a binary semaphore?
options: A mutex has an owner: the thread that locked it is the one that should unlock it
A mutex can count to 10, a binary semaphore cannot
A binary semaphore can only be used by one process ever
There is no difference of any kind
questions.answer: A mutex has an owner: the thread that locked it is the one that should unlock it
questions.explanation: A mutex is for mutual exclusion and has ownership. A binary semaphore is a signaling tool: any thread may release it, even one that never acquired it. Both hold values 0 or 1, which is why they are confused.

questions.text: What does this single-threaded program print?
options: true / true / true / 0
true / true / false / 1
true / false / false / 1
true / true / false / 2
questions.explanation: The semaphore starts with 2 permits, so two tryAcquire calls succeed and the third fails without blocking. release() returns one permit, so availablePermits() is 1.

questions.text: A server may hold at most 5 simultaneous database connections. Extra requests should wait their turn. What do you use?
options: A mutex around the whole request
A boolean flag checked in a loop
A counting semaphore initialized to 5
A binary semaphore initialized to 0
questions.explanation: Each request acquires a permit and releases it when done, so up to 5 run at once and the rest block. A mutex would allow only one at a time, and a semaphore starting at 0 would block everyone.

questions.text: Two threads each run count++ one thousand times on a shared int with no synchronization. Why can the final value be less than 2000?
options: Java limits an int to 1000 increments
The JVM runs only one thread at a time
count++ is atomic, so the result is always 2000
count++ is read, add, write; interleaved steps can overwrite each other's updates
questions.answer: count++ is read, add, write; interleaved steps can overwrite each other's updates
questions.explanation: Both threads can read the same old value, each add 1 and write back the same result, losing one increment. This is a race condition. Wrapping the increment in a mutex makes the three steps one critical section.

questions.text: Thread B must not run step 2 until thread A has finished step 1. Which semaphore setup enforces this?
options: Initial value 1; A acquires it first, B releases it
Initial value 0; A releases it after step 1, B acquires it before step 2
Initial value 0; B releases it after step 1, A acquires it
Initial value 5; both threads acquire it before starting
questions.answer: Initial value 0; A releases it after step 1, B acquires it before step 2
questions.explanation: A semaphore at 0 makes B block on acquire until A signals with release. Starting at 1 or more lets B pass immediately, so the ordering would not be guaranteed.
